title: MAKUC AND OTHERS v. SLOVENIA
summary: In Makuc and Others v. Slovenia, the applicants—eleven individuals, including Mr Milan Makuc and others—were former citizens of Yugoslavia, several of whom identified as Roma or belonged to other groups encompassed by the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. Their case against Slovenia centred on the vulnerability of “the erased,” a group that included many Roma, who lost their legal status and fundamental rights following Slovenia’s independence. After Slovenia declared independence in 1991, the applicants, who had been permanent residents, failed to apply for Slovenian citizenship within the required timeframe. On 26 February 1992, their names were deleted from the Register of Permanent Residents, rendering them foreigners overnight and stripping them of access to healthcare, employment, and social security. Some faced expulsion or were unable to regularise their status for years. The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under several articles, including Articles 8 (private and family life), 13 (effective remedy), and 14 (non-discrimination), but ultimately declared the case partly inadmissible, finding that domestic remedies had not been exhausted. Although no violation was found, the case highlighted the precarious situation of Roma and other minorities affected by administrative erasure. This case remains significant as it drew international attention to the systemic exclusion faced by Roma and Travellers in post-socialist Europe, particularly during periods of state succession and legal transition.
